# Dealing with Text: stringr {#sec-stringr}

::: {.callout-note}
**Proposed chapter scope:** String manipulation with `stringr` as the foundation for working with text data. Covers pattern matching (regex), string detection, extraction, replacement, and splitting. Focuses on cleaning and preparing raw text before analysis rather than analysis itself.
:::

Many interesting (computational) social science data sets have textual elements.
This can e.g. the contents of online posts or reviews,
official documents, reports, or party manifestoes,
but also open survey questions or question metadata. 

Very often, we need to clean, preprocess and/or analyse this textual data. 
This chapter will take the first steps in this by introducing the tidyverse `stringr` package,
which can handle most of the cleaning functions such as normalizing, filtering and extracting parts of textual columns. 
In the next chapters we will look at other parts of the pipeline: scraping and reading textual data (@sec-scraping),
analysing Text as Data (@sec-textasdata), and using LLMs as an analysis tool (@sec-llm). 

## Data for this chapter: US Elections on Bluesky

As an example data set for this chapter, 
we will use a collection of Bluesky posts about the 2024 US elections (see [the book's github repository](https://github.com/vanatteveldt/r4css/blob/main/data/README.md#us-elections-bluesky-posts) for the R code used to scrape these posts).
To make things easier, we will only keep the date, author and text columns:

```{webr}
#| warning: false
library(tidyverse)
download.file("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/vanatteveldt/r4css/refs/heads/main/data/bluesky_us_elections_2024.csv", "bluesky_us_elections_2024.csv")
posts <- read_csv("bluesky_us_elections_2024.csv")|>
  select(author=author_name, date=created_at, likes=like_count, text)
head(posts)
```

```{webr}
#| setup: true
#| exercise: ['demo_detect_trump', 'demo_detect_lower', 'demo_length_likes', 'demo_squish_count', 'demo_hashtag_detect', 'demo_hashtag_extract', 'demo_hashtag_remove', 'demo_mention_anonymize', 'demo_hashtag_extract_all', 'demo_hashtag_toy', 'demo_dotall']
library(tidyverse)
posts <- read_csv("data/bluesky_us_elections_2024.csv") |>
  select(author=author_name, date=created_at, likes=like_count, text)
```

## Using `stringr` for basic text cleaning and processing {#sec-basicstringr}

As a first step, we will look at a number of functions from the `stringr`
package for detecting and counting whether a text contains a specific word or substring. This is very useful for cleaning and exploring data. 

### Who do people post about? Using `str_detect` in `filter`

A first question we might ask is how much people post about a candidate, for example Donald Trump. We can use `str_detect` to check whether a text contains a specific substring, and use that to filter the posts:

```{webr}
#| exercise: demo_detect_trump
trump_posts <- posts |> filter(str_detect(text, "Trump"))
head(trump_posts)
str_glue("Total number of posts: {nrow(posts)}")
str_glue("Number of posts about trump: {nrow(trump_posts)}")
```


:::{.callout-note title="str_glue"}
In the example above, we used `str_glue` to display the number of posts in a nice way. You've actually already seen this in @sec-vis-why, where we used it to create a nice label in a graph.

`str_glue` is a very useful function for building a text by 'glueing' calculated values (such as `{nrow(posts)}`) into a text. Technically, all R code within curly braces (`{}`) will be evaluated and inserted into the text. 

A small caveat: if the code produces multiple values, this will result in multiple texts being produced. This is useful if you use `str_glue` within a `mutate` call, as it will produce a value for each row, but might be surprising if you use it to quickly print something like above.
You can use `str_glue("Count to three: {str_c(1:3, collapse=',')}")` if you want to include multiple values in a single string: this 'collapses' multiple values (1, 2 and 3 in this case) into a single string `"1,2,3"`.
:::


As you can see, about 25% of the posts mention Trump -- or rather, contain the specific sequence of characters `T-r-u-m-p`. This will not find `trump`, but will find `#Trump`, `DonaldTrump`. To also find matches of `trump`, an easy trick is to call `str_to_lower(text)` to lowercase the whole text column:

```{webr}
#| exercise: demo_detect_lower
posts |> filter(str_detect(str_to_lower(text), "trump"))
```

Which finds about 300 extra mentions (which could of course also include false positives, e.g. trump used a verb or trumpet as a musical instrument)

::: {.callout-note title="All the str_ functions"}
As you might have noticed, all functions introduced above started with `str_`:
`str_detect`, `str_glue`, and `str_to_lower`. 
This naming convention holds for (almost) all functions in `stringr`. 
This makes it easy to find them in Rstudio: 
just type `str_` and press tab or control_space, and you get an overview of all 
the functions for dealing with text. 
See the table near the end of this chapter for an overview of useful stringr functions. 
:::

### Basic string functions in a data frame

Next to filtering, it can be useful to use `stringr` within a `mutate` call
to calculate properties of the data. For example, we could count the length of all posts, and check if longer posts get more likes:

```{webr}
#| exercise: demo_length_likes
posts <- posts |>
  mutate(length=str_length(text))
cor.test(posts$length, posts$likes)
```

We can also use `str_count` to count how often a fragment occurs within a text.
If we count the number of spaces, we get a decent approximation of the number of words in each post (but see the callout below on characters vs words).

Before we do this, we should probably normalize the whitespace in the posts.
The function `str_trim` can be used to remove ('trim') all whitespace at the start and end of a text. 
We will go a step further and use `str_squish`, which trims the text but also replaces all consecutive whitespaces by a single space, i.e. it replaces newlines, tabs, multiple spaces or any combination of these by a single space. 

```{webr}
#| exercise: demo_squish_count
posts <- posts |>
  mutate(text_normalized=str_squish(text),
         length=str_length(text_normalized),
         nwords=str_count(text_normalized, " "))
head(posts)
```

### Exercise: Talk of the town?

{{< include exercises/_ch09_ex_mentions_over_time.qmd >}}

::: {.callout-note title="Analysis of texts: characters or words?"}

In the examples and exercise above, we use the `str_` functions 
to perform simple text analyses by counting mentions of candidates. 

This works, but has very clear limits because `stringr` fundamentally works on **characters**, while a lot of our analyses talk about words. 
As mentioned, `str_detect(str_to_lower(text), "trump")` will match trumpet
(as well as `"#trump"`, `"STRUMP"` and `"Strumpfhose"`). The reason is that `stringr` sees `Strumpfhose` as a sequence of characters `S-t-r-u-m-p-f...`, and these characters contain the sequence `t-r-u-m-p`, so it matches. `stringr` doesn't really know what a word is, and doesn't really care either. 

This can be solved to a degree by using more sophisticated matching rules, as explained below, but these solutions are relatively brittle and address the sympton rather than the cause: often, we would like to analyse words rather than characters. @sec-textasdata will address this problem head-on by first **tokenizing** a text into words, and then using analyses on the words.

None of this makes the `stringr` package any less relevant:
Functions like `str_detect`, `str_trim` and `str_count` are still very useful for filtering and cleaning texts -- and in fact many of the analyses in @sec-textasdata will use these functions either before or after the tokenization to clean the text and analyse the extracted words. 
:::

## Finding, removing and replacing simple patterns {#sec-findreplace}

The code above showed how you can detect and count literal substrings.
The `stringr` functions are much more powerful than that, however,
as you can also search for *patterns* containing wildcards.

For now, we will just introduce some very basic patterns, that are however already quite powerful. For example, the code below will use the pattern `"#\\w+"` to filter on posts containing at least one hashtag:

```{webr}
#| exercise: demo_hashtag_detect
posts_with_tags <- posts |> filter(str_detect(text, "#\\w+"))
head(posts_with_tags)
str_glue("{nrow(posts_with_tags)} out of {nrow(posts)} posts contained a hash tag")
```

So it looks like all posts contain at least one hash tag. This is actually not a coincidence -- why do you think this could be the case?

::: {.callout-note title="Regular expressions?"}
The pattern introduced above (`#\\w+`) may look weird, overly complex, or suspiciously like a cartoon curseword. But it's actually a very standardized and useful way to express character patterns called **regular expressions** (or *regex*, for friends)

Although this will be explained in much more detail in @sec-regex,
it is useful to explain at least a little bit of what is going on. 
In a regex, most characters simply match that character, which is why we could use `"trump"` above to simply search for the word "trump", or actually the sequence of characters `t-r-u-m-p`. 

The `\\w`, however, is a kind of wildcard called a *character class* rather than a literal sequence of `\` and `w` characters. 
This specific class matches 'word characters' defined as letters and numbers (and curiously the underscore `_`). So, `#\\w` would match a literal hash sign (`#`), followed by a letter, number, or underscore. 

The last part, `+`, is a quantifier which reads "one or more": it means that the preceding character (in this case, the `\\w` word character class) is required but may be repeated as often as desired. So, the total pattern `#\\w+` matches a literal hash sign, followed by one or more word characters, which is a fair approximation of a hash tag.

By using combinations of character classes and quantifiers, you can make patterns for many useful things such as hashtags, zip codes, phone numbers, email addresses, etc. 
:::

### Extracting a pattern with `str_extract`

More usefully, we can use `str_extract` to extract the (first) hashtag in each post, and store it as a new column. This allows us to get an overview of hashtags in the posts:

```{webr}
#| exercise: demo_hashtag_extract
posts |>
  mutate(tag=str_extract(text, "#\\w+")) |>
  count(tag) |>
  arrange(desc(n))
```

So, the corpus is dominated by the hashtag `#Election2024` --
as you might have guessed above this was used to select relevant posts, so each post will contain this tag. 

Note that the reason why the total is lower than the total number of posts is that the code above only extracts the *first* occurrence of a pattern, so in the other posts another tag was used before that tag (and see @sec-extractall for `str_extract_all` to extract all tags)

### Removing parts of a text with `str_remove_all`

Since the occurrence of this particular hashtag is not informative, let's clean the data first by lowercasing it, and then removing that hashtag using `str_remove_all`, followed by the same code as above:

```{webr}
#| exercise: demo_hashtag_remove
posts |>
  mutate(text=str_to_lower(text),
         text=str_remove_all(text, "#election2024"),
         tag=str_extract(text, "#\\w+")) |>
  count(tag) |>
  arrange(desc(n))
```

This is more informative: a number of posts had no other hashtags (giving a `NA` for the extraction), and after the somewhat generic `#politics` and `#vote` tags we see hashtags for the two main candidates, mostly balanced. 

### Replacing text with `str_replace_all`

Next to removing text, we can replace parts of a text with `str_replace_all(text, pattern, replacement)`. For example, we can 'anonymize' the at-mentions by replacing all word characters after an at sign by an `ANONYMIZED` placeholder 
(using `str_squish` to make it easier to read the results):

```{webr}
#| exercise: demo_mention_anonymize
posts |>
  filter(str_detect(text, "@\\w+")) |>
  mutate(
    text = str_squish(text),
    anonymized=str_replace_all(text, "@\\w+", "@ANONYMIZED")) |>
  select(anonymized)
```

Note that this only replaces the at-mention until a non-word character appears. Since bluesky names often contain domain names (e.g. `@example.bsky.social`) this will only replace the first part and leave the domain intact,
which might or might not be a desired effect.
For more powerful ways of specifying patterns, see @sec-regex below. 

:::{.callout-note title="Matching periods: escaping and fixed()"}
As noted above, the `\\w` pattern matches letters, numbers, and underscore, but not the dots in a domain name. 
Confusingly, the period character (`.`) also does not (just) match a literal dot:
it is a character class itself, and matches every possible character (apart from line breaks). So,
`@\\w+.bsky.social` matches all at-mentions in this domain, but would also match `@\\w+_bsky_social` and even `@\\w+ bsky social`.

For this case it's probably not a big deal, as those patterns are unlikely to appear. But let's try searching for `U.S.`:

```{webr}
#| exercise: demo_dotall
us_posts <- posts |> filter(str_detect(text, 'U.S.'))
str_glue("Total number of matches: {nrow(us_posts)}")
print("Text of the 23rd match:")
us_posts$text[23]
```

As you can see, this gives 130 matches. But not all of them actually contain the string `U.S.`, for example the 23rd match printed here. Why did that post match?

The answer, of course, is that `.` is a wildcard, so the pattern `U.S.` matched the word `RUSSIAN`!

To remedy this, you have two options. The easiest is to enclose the whole pattern in a `fixed()` function: `str_detect(text, fixed('U.S.'))` tells R to actually not use a regular expression pattern, but a fixed substring. The alternative is to place a double backslash before each period: `U\\.S\\.`, a practice known as *escaping* (again, see @sec-regex below for more detail). Try either pattern yourself in the code above - it should return 102 rows instead of the original 130. 
:::

### Finding multiple occurrences with `str_extract_all` {#sec-extractall}

Earlier, we tried to analyse hashtag usage in the US Election posts,
noting the limitation that `str_extract` only extracts the first occurrence of a pattern.

After seeing the examples with `str_remove_all` and `str_replace_all`, 
you may have guesses that there is also a function called `str_extract_all` -- and you would be right. 

The complication is that this of course can return multiple results per row, which does not really fit with the idea of a column in a data frame: a cell normally contains only a single value. This can be solved by using `unnest_longer`, for example to do a complete count of all hashtags:

```{webr}
#| exercise: demo_hashtag_extract_all
posts |>
  mutate(tag=str_extract_all(text, "#\\w+")) |>
  unnest_longer(tag) |>
  count(tag) |>
  arrange(desc(n))
```

Technically, `str_extract_all` produces a 'list column', i.e. a column with a data type list. Since that is not very useful for analysis, we *unnest* the list column into a long format: every value becomes a row, so if two hashtags were found the row will be repeated for each hashtag, with only the `tag` column being different and containing a single tag. 

To make this more explicit, the following toy example shows the results for each step:

```{webr}
#| exercise: demo_hashtag_toy
toy <- tibble(text="Three hashtags: #trump #harris #biden")
toy <- toy |> mutate(tag=str_extract_all(text, "#\\w+"))
print("Result after extract_all:")
print(toy)

toy <- toy |> unnest_longer(tag)
print("Result after unnest_longer:")
print(toy)
```
